findings.title: readBytes allocates an attacker-controlled 32-bit length before reading any payload (unbounded heap allocation)
findings.impact: A peer can force a ~2 GiB heap allocation with about nine bytes on the wire, repeatedly, on the connection's I/O thread. The result is OutOfMemoryError or sustained GC thrash in the client JVM - a denial of service of the whole hosting application, not just of the connection. Reachable from a malicious or compromised broker, and from an on-path attacker whenever TLS is not in use, through any longstr method argument, any 'S' or 'x' field value inside a header table, and the longstr content-header properties.
findings.evidence: readBytes does `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()); if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) { final byte[] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]; in.readFully(buffer); ... }`. The length comes straight off the wire and the array is allocated BEFORE readFully is attempted, so the allocation happens even when the declared length is far larger than the bytes that could possibly follow - the frame-level size cap never prevents it, it only guarantees the subsequent read fails. Nothing cross-checks contentLength against in.available() or against any configured maximum; the sole guard, `< Integer.MAX_VALUE`, still permits 2147483646 bytes.
findings.recommendation: Validate before allocating. In the normal call path the frame payload is already fully buffered, so `if (contentLength > in.available()) throw new MalformedFrameException(...)` is both cheap and exact; additionally cap against a configurable maximum (the same knob that bounds inbound message body size) so the check still holds for any stream handed to the public constructor. Allocate only after the length has passed both checks.

findings.title: Field-table and field-array decoding recurses without a depth limit (StackOverflowError from a single frame)
findings.impact: One small, otherwise well-formed frame drives the decoder into unbounded recursion and kills the connection thread with StackOverflowError. Because that is an Error and not an IOException, it bypasses the MalformedFrameException/IOException handling the frame layer uses to fail a channel or connection cleanly, so it surfaces as an unhandled crash of the I/O loop rather than as a protocol error, and connection state is left uncleaned. Each level additionally allocates two wrapper streams plus a HashMap or ArrayList, making the same input a memory amplifier.
findings.evidence: readFieldValue case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable, which loops calling readFieldValue; case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray, which loops calling readFieldValue. Neither path carries a depth counter or any nesting limit. A nested table costs 6 bytes per level on the wire (0x00 short-string name length, 'F', 4-byte table length) and a nested array 5 bytes per level ('A', 4-byte length), so a payload well under the default 128 KiB frame_max encodes more than 20000 levels of nesting - far past the default JVM stack depth.
findings.recommendation: Thread an explicit depth argument through readFieldValue/readTable/readArray, increment it on entry to the 'F' and 'A' cases, and throw MalformedFrameException beyond a small fixed maximum (real field tables nest one or two levels; 16-32 is generous). Keep the existing public entry points as thin wrappers that start the depth at zero.

findings.title: Tables and arrays are decoded by draining available() with no check that the declared length was consumed, so a truncated table is accepted as valid
findings.impact: A peer that declares a table length running past the end of the enclosing frame, and places the cut on an entry boundary, gets a partial map returned as if it were the complete, valid header set - no exception, no log line. The receiving application then observes headers the sender never sent, most dangerously with a security-relevant header silently absent, which turns a check written as 'if the header says X, deny' into a pass. The mirror case (a declared length shorter than the bytes actually written) leaves the enclosing stream positioned mid-value, desynchronising the remaining arguments or content-header properties of that frame. Separately, the available()-driven loop makes correctness depend on the underlying stream being fully buffered, and the ValueReader constructor is public and accepts any DataInputStream - including a socket-backed one, where available() can legitimately return 0 mid-table and truncate a perfectly valid table.
findings.evidence: readTable: `DataInputStream tableIn = new DataInputStream(new TruncatedInputStream(in, tableLength)); while(tableIn.available() > 0) { ... }`, and readArray at line 244 repeats the identical `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` pattern. tableLength and length are never compared against the bytes actually remaining, and after the loop nothing asserts that exactly the declared number of bytes was consumed. Truncation only raises EOFException when the cut lands mid-value; when it lands between entries the loop simply ends and returns the partial result.
findings.recommendation: Reject up front when the declared length exceeds the bytes available in the frame payload, and after the loop verify the truncated stream was consumed exactly, throwing MalformedFrameException otherwise. Drive the loop from a byte counter derived from the declared length rather than from available(), so the decoder no longer silently depends on the stream being buffered.

findings.title: Malformed input escapes the decoder as an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException instead of MalformedFrameException
findings.impact: A peer that declares a length of 2147483647 or more triggers an unchecked exception out of the decode path. Callers that wrap decoding in `catch (IOException)` to fail the channel or connection as a protocol error do not catch it, so it propagates through the I/O loop to a generic uncaught-exception path, if any. Hostile input that is simply a malformed frame therefore produces an inconsistent, harder-to-diagnose failure mode than every other malformed frame, and can leave connection state uncleaned.
findings.evidence: readBytes: `} else { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported"); }`. The only other rejection in this class - the unknown type tag at line 217 - correctly uses MalformedFrameException, which extends IOException.
findings.recommendation: Throw MalformedFrameException here, including the offending length in the message, so every rejection of hostile wire input leaves the decoder through the same checked-exception contract the frame layer already handles.

findings.title: Duplicate field names in a table are resolved first-wins and the duplicate is silently discarded (parser differential)
findings.impact: Where the broker, a plugin, or another AMQP implementation resolves a repeated field name last-wins - or rejects the table outright - this client resolves it first-wins and reports nothing. Anyone able to append a second copy of a header can therefore make the client read a different value for that header than the component that made the routing or authorization decision on it. Because the duplicate is dropped with no exception, no counter and no log line, the divergence is invisible to operators.
findings.evidence: readTable: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` - second and later occurrences of a name are fully parsed and then thrown away with no signal of any kind.
findings.recommendation: Reject a table that repeats a field name with MalformedFrameException, which is the safe reading for a wire decoder and removes the differential entirely. If backwards compatibility forbids that, keep the behaviour but document it on the public readTable() and emit a warning so the condition is at least observable.

findings.title: readTimestamp multiplies an attacker-controlled long by 1000 with no overflow check
findings.impact: Any AMQP timestamp above roughly 9.22e15 wraps silently, letting a peer choose the sign and magnitude of the Date the application receives - a far-future timestamp can be delivered as a far-past one. Applications that use the timestamp property for expiry, replay-window or ordering decisions get a value that passes their check when it should have failed it.
findings.evidence: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);` - a raw 64-bit wire value multiplied in long arithmetic, with no range validation, no overflow detection and no rejection path.
findings.recommendation: Use Math.multiplyExact(seconds, 1000L) and convert the resulting ArithmeticException into a MalformedFrameException, or range-check the seconds value before multiplying.

findings.title: readTable returns an immutable map for an empty table and a mutable one otherwise, so a remote peer decides whether the caller's map is writable
findings.impact: The public readTable() has an inconsistent contract that is selected by wire input. Application code that mutates the returned header map - a common pattern when re-publishing a message with an added or stripped header - works in every test where headers are present, then throws UnsupportedOperationException in production the first time a peer sends an empty header table. A peer can trigger that path deliberately, and the exception surfaces inside consumer callbacks where it typically aborts delivery handling.
findings.evidence: readTable: `if (tableLength == 0) return Collections.emptyMap();` while the non-empty path returns `new HashMap<String, Object>()`. Both are returned through the same `public final Map<String, Object> readTable()` at line 252, whose signature and Javadoc promise nothing about mutability.
findings.recommendation: Return one kind of map from both paths - either `new HashMap<>()` for the empty case, or make the whole method return an unmodifiable view - and state the chosen contract in the Javadoc of the public readTable().

findings.title: amqp-client forces netty-transport, netty-codec and netty-handler onto every consumer's classpath
findings.impact: Netty is a large, network-facing library with a steady CVE cadence. Declaring it compile-scope and non-optional makes it a mandatory transitive dependency of every application that uses this client, including the large majority that never select the Netty frame handler. Those applications inherit every future Netty advisory, must track and override the version themselves, and show up in their own scanners as exposed to vulnerabilities in code they never load. It also risks a version conflict with the Netty an application already uses.
findings.evidence: In the dependencies block, io.netty:netty-transport, netty-codec and netty-handler (lines 381-394) are the only pluggable-integration dependencies declared with default compile scope and no <optional>true</optional>. Every other pluggable integration in the same block - metrics-core, micrometer-core, opentelemetry-api and jackson-databind (lines 396-418) - is marked optional. The build's own spotless configuration confirms Netty backs one frame-handler implementation among others (src/main/java/com/rabbitmq/client/impl/NettyFrameHandlerFactory.java).
findings.recommendation: Mark the three Netty artifacts <optional>true</optional>, matching the treatment of the other integrations, and document that the Netty-based transport requires the user to add netty-transport/codec/handler explicitly. If Netty is in fact the default transport and cannot be made optional, say so in the POM so the mandatory exposure is a recorded decision rather than an oversight.

findings.title: Build and test dependencies pinned to end-of-life branches that no longer receive fixes
findings.impact: None of these ship in the published jar, so downstream users are not exposed; the risk is to the build and CI hosts and to the project's own supply chain. Any vulnerability found in these branches will never be fixed there, so the only remedy is a major-version migration made under time pressure. The Groovy case is the most relevant: groovy-all runs on every build during generate-sources, so it is code executing on developer and CI machines, not just in tests.
findings.evidence: logback.version 1.2.13 (line 64, test scope) - the 1.2.x branch predates the 1.3/1.5 lines and receives no further fixes. jetty.version 9.4.58.v20250814 (line 70, test scope) - Jetty 9.4 is past community end of life. groovy.all.version 2.4.21 (line 81) is supplied to the groovy-maven-plugin execution bound to generate-sources at line 615, so an end-of-life Groovy 2.4 runtime executes on every build. slf4j.version 1.7.36 (line 58) is compile scope and does ship, though the facade itself has no known vulnerability.
findings.recommendation: Move logback to a supported line for the test classpath, move the Jetty test dependency to a supported major, and move the codegen execution to a maintained Groovy (4.x) or replace the Groovy shim, which exists only to invoke codegen.py, with a direct exec-maven-plugin invocation and drop the Groovy dependency entirely. Add a scheduled dependency scan to CI so end-of-life pins surface without a manual review.

findings.title: Short strings are decoded with lenient UTF-8 replacement, so invalid byte sequences become silently corrupted table keys
findings.impact: Field-table keys and other short strings that are not valid UTF-8 are accepted rather than rejected, with malformed sequences replaced by U+FFFD. Distinct byte sequences therefore collapse onto the same String key, and combined with the first-wins rule of F-005 the later of two colliding keys is discarded without any error. The application ends up with a key it cannot map back to what was on the wire, and cannot distinguish a corrupted header name from a legitimate one.
findings.evidence: readShortstr: `return new String(b, "utf-8");`. The String(byte[], String) constructor uses CodingErrorAction.REPLACE and has no way to report malformed input; nothing validates b beforehand.
findings.recommendation: Decode through a CharsetDecoder for StandardCharsets.UTF_8 configured with CodingErrorAction.REPORT and convert CharacterCodingException into MalformedFrameException, so invalid wire data is rejected rather than silently mangled.
